---
title: "Google Trends: Do richer countries look more to the future?"
author: "Dr. David Garcia"
---

This exercise reproduces the findings of the article "Quantifying the Advantage of Looking Forward" <http://www.nature.com/articles/srep00350>. According to the results, the GDP per capita of countries is positively correlated to how much their population searches in Google for the next year, relative to how much they search for the previous year. This ratio is called the Future Orientation Index (FOI). So for example for the year 2017 the FOI can be calculated as: FOI = number of searches for the term "2018" / number of searches for the term "2016".

You can find the markdown files and data for this exercise in this folder (`Session03_RetrievingData/Exercise1`)

# 1. Package installation and setup

For this task you will need to install the WDI package. The WDI package gives you access to data of the World Bank's World Development Indicators.

**1.1 Install the WDI package**

Run the following commands in your R console to install the WDI package
```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
# Your code here
install.packages("WDI")
install.packages("dplyr")
```

**1.2 Load the WDI library**

In the following chunk, load the WDI library
```{r loading}
library(WDI)
library(dplyr)

```

**1.3 Set working directory**

Check that the working directory of R Studio is the same one where you have the Markdown file. You can set it automatically with this:
```{r wd, eval=FALSE}
setwd(dirname(rstudioapi::getSourceEditorContext()$path))
```

# 2. World Bank Data

**2.1 Download WDI data**


From the WDI we need three indicators:

- Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per capita corrected by the Purchase Power Parity (PPP in current or 2005 international $, "NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD")

- The number of Internet users (per 100 people, "IT.NET.USER.ZS")

- The total population (described as "Population, Total", "SP.POP.TOTL")

In the following code chunk, download all data (including extras) for all countries in year 2014.
```{r WDIdata}
# Your code here
df <- WDI(country = "all", 
          indicator = c("NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD", 
                        "IT.NET.USER.ZS", 
                        "SP.POP.TOTL"), 
          start = 2014, 
          end = 2014, 
          extra = TRUE)
head(df)

```

**2.2 Clean WDI data**

Some entries are not complete and some others are not countries, but regions. In the following code chunk, make sure that you only use complete rows (use the complete.cases function) and ignore groups of countries and regions by deleting rows 'Aggregates' on the region column.

```{r cleanData}

df <- df[complete.cases(df),]
df <- df[df$region != "Aggregates", ]
head(df)
```


**2.3 Select countries with more than 5 million internet users**
In the following code chunk, calculate the value of a new column with the estimated amount of internet users in the country.
Filter out countries with fewer than 5 million internet users (as reported in the original article).

```{r selectCountries}
# Your code here
df$internetUsers <- df$SP.POP.TOTL * df$IT.NET.USER.ZS / 100
df <- df[df$internetUsers >= 5000000, ]
df <- filter_out(df,internetUsers <5000000)
head(df)
```

\newpage

# 3. The Future Orientation Index in Google Trends

**3.1 Download data from Google Trends**

You can download the data from Google Trends following these steps:

- log out from your Google account or set its language to English
- Go to trends.google.com and search for 2013
- add 2015 as a search term
- Select custom time range: full year: 2014
- Set the region to "Worldwide". You can also try with this link:
<https://trends.google.com/trends/explore?date=2014-01-01%202014-12-31&q=2013,2015>
- Go to the map at "Compared breakdown by region" and tick on "include low search volume regions"
- On the top right menu click the download button to get a geoMap.csv file

Load the .csv file and clean its format with the following code chunk

```{r trendsData}
trends <- read.csv("geoMap1.csv", skip = 2)
head(trends)
# gets cols exept for Land:
x <- setdiff(names(trends), "Land") # Land due to me failing to switch the lanuage
trends[x] <- lapply(trends[x], function(col) { # Turning percent string to float
  col <- gsub("%", "", col)      
  col <- gsub(",", ".", col)     
  col <- as.numeric(col)
})       
head(trends)
```

**3.2 Calculate the Future Orientation Index**

In the following code chunk, make a new column in the google trends dataframe with the Future Orientation Index, which is the ratio between the search volume for 2015 and 2013 in 2014 for each country

```{r FOI}
trends$FOI <- trends$X2015 / trends$X2013
head(trends)
```

**3.3 Merge with World Bank data**

Merge the WDI and google trends data frames, using the name of the country. (Hint: use 
"merge" or "inner_join")
```{r MergeData}
merged_data <- merge(df, trends, by.x = "country", by.y = "Land")

# -- Claude --
cat("WDI rådata:", nrow(df), "rader,", ncol(df), "kolumner\n")
cat("Trends rådata:", nrow(trends), "rader,", ncol(trends), "kolumner\n")
cat("Trends utan NA i FOI:", sum(!is.na(trends$FOI)), "\n")
nrow(trends) + nrow(df)
head(merged_data)
cat("After the old merge method:", nrow(merged_data), "rader,", ncol(merged_data), "kolumner\n")

# --/> claude --- There is a large diffrence in collumns so some are dropped due to name missmatch, below is pasted fix from claude
library(countrycode)

trends$iso2c <- countrycode(trends$Land, "country.name", "iso2c",
                            custom_match = c("Kosovo" = "XK", "Türkiye" = "TR"))

merged_data <- merge(df, trends, by = "iso2c") 
cat("After the new merge method:", nrow(merged_data), "rader,", ncol(merged_data), "kolumner\n") # <- can be concluded that the issue lies with the old merge method

nrow(merged_data)
anti_join(df, trends, by = "iso2c")$country   # länder som tappades
```

# 4. Testing the correlation between GDP and FOI

**4.1 Visualize FOI vs GDP**

Now that you have the FOI and GDP per capita, PPP value for each country, you can make a scatter plot of FOI vs GDP
```{r scatterplot}
plot(merged_data$NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, merged_data$FOI,
     xlab = "GDP per capita (PPP)",
     ylab = "Future Orientation Index (FOI)",
     pch = 19,          
     col = "black")     
```

**4.2 Measure Pearson's correlation**

In the following chunk, calculate Pearson's correlation coefficient between GDP and FOI
```{r correlation}
correlation <- cor(merged_data$NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, merged_data$FOI, method = "pearson")
correlation
```

\newpage

**4.3 Measure correlation after shuffling**

What happens if we shuffle the data (e.g. shuffle the FOIs) and repeat the above analysis? Do you find any difference between the two plots and two Pearson's correlation coefficients?
- Not any of stastical significance 
```{r shuffletest}
# Your code here
merged_data$shuffFOI <- sample(merged_data$FOI)
correlation <- cor(merged_data$NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, merged_data$shuffFOI, method = "pearson")
correlation
plot(merged_data$NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, merged_data$shuffFOI,
     xlab = "GDP per capita (PPP)",
     ylab = "Future Orientation Index (FOI)",
     pch = 19,          
     col = "black")     
```

Answer: 
The main diffrence can be seen in the pearson coefficent as it is now  random and thus lies very close to 0, and is substationally diffrent from the test results which strengthens the result that the two are correlated.

- What result do you get if you use other years? What if you choose one of the earliest years in Google trends?
- How do results change if you use a threshold other than 5 million Internet users?
- Is future orientation generating wealth? Or is it wealth that enables looking to the future?
- Is the FOI really measuring Future Orientation? Could it be something else?

```{r extra tests}

merged_data <- filter(merged_data, NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD < 80000)
plot(merged_data$NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, merged_data$FOI,
     xlab = "GDP per capita (PPP)",
     ylab = "Future Orientation Index (FOI)",
     pch = 19,          
     col = "black")     
```
